documents.text:
The query is forwarded byte for byte as the client sent it, so a signed URL keeps its signature. Only when a handler changed the arguments through `QueryArgs()` is it the changed arguments, as fasthttp serializes them; reading them, as `c.Query()` does, changes nothing. `Balancer` puts the original request line back once the upstream has answered, so `c.OriginalURL()` in a middleware that runs afterwards is unchanged.

- `Balancer` reaches each server with the port and the scheme it was configured with, whichever the request arrived on: an entry without a port is dialed on 80 (`http`) or 443 (`https`), and an `https` server works behind a plain-HTTP listener, as an `http` server does behind a TLS one. With a custom `Config.Client` the `HostClient`s are yours, and so is the scheme they expect: set it on the request in `ModifyRequest`.
- `Balancer` dials the configured host and forwards the target as is, so every entry in `Servers` must be a scheme and host only. An entry with a path, userinfo, query or fragment panics at startup with `ErrUpstreamNotOrigin` instead of dropping that part silently, which would have left `http://backend/api` reaching all of the upstream. An entry without a scheme, such as `backend:8080`, is read as `http://backend:8080`, and a lone trailing slash (`http://backend/`) is ignored. `DomainForward` and `BalancerForward` prepend the path of their upstream URL, and the joined path keeps the upstream host pinned in configuration whatever the request contains: `//attacker.example/path`, `@attacker` and `/foo://hijack.example` all stay paths. Both parts keep their escapes as written, so behind `http://backend/my%20app` the target `/pub/..%3B/admin` is forwarded as `/my%20app/pub/..%3B/admin`, not as `/my%20app/pub/..;/admin`.
- `Balancer` answers `400 Bad Request` for an absolute-form request whose request line names another host than the `Host` header, such as `GET http://public.example/x` with `Host: internal.example`, or that has no `Host` header. The host of the request line is the one `c.Host()` reports and `app.Domain` and `hostauthorization` match ([RFC 9112 Section 3.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112#section-3.2.2)), while the upstream is addressed by the `Host` header. A client has to send the same host in both ([RFC 9112 Section 3.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112#section-3.2)), and such a request is forwarded; the two are compared without regard to case, and a port that is empty or the default of the scheme counts as none, so `http://public.example:80/x` with `Host: public.example` is forwarded as well. Only a host name or an IP address, with an optional port, can match: a host that holds an escape or any other byte is refused even when both spell it alike, since the upstream receives the `Host` header decoded while `c.Host()` may keep the escape. RFC 9112 has a proxy replace the received `Host` with the host of the line instead, but at this point the header may hold a `Host` the application set in an earlier middleware, which a request line must not override. An application that sets the `Host` header before `Balancer` therefore gets `400` for every absolute-form request whose line names another host than the one it set, even when the client sent the same host in both; set the upstream `Host` in `ModifyRequest` instead, which runs after this check. An HTTP/1.0 absolute-form request without a `Host` header is refused before `ModifyRequest` runs.
- `Balancer` answers a request whose `Host` header carries userinfo, such as `svc:pw@backend`, with `400 Bad Request`. fasthttp would read the userinfo as credentials and send them upstream as a `Basic` `Authorization` header, replacing one the application had set.

`ErrUpstreamHostUnresolvable` is new: a name that cannot be resolved, or that resolves to no address, is rejected with an error that matches it and `ErrUpstreamHostBlocked` both, and `errors.As` finds the `*net.DNSError` of the lookup. A host with only IPv6 addresses and `DialDualStack` off fails with an error that matches neither, where it matched `ErrUpstreamHostBlocked` before. An address `net/url` cannot parse is rejected with `ErrUpstreamHostInvalid` and the `*url.Error` wrapped beside it, so the message of that error carries the parse error. The time `DoTimeout`, `DoDeadline` or `Config.Timeout` allows bounds the lookup and the connects of the request as well; a connect that nothing bounds has five seconds, as before.

`Balancer`, `DomainForward` and `BalancerForward` forward the path the router matched, `c.Path()`, followed by the query as the client sent it, instead of the request line as it arrived. Spellings such as `/public/..%2Fadmin/secret` and `//admin/secret`, which fasthttp's normalization of the raw request line turned into `/admin/secret` on the way to the upstream, are answered with `400 Bad Request`, since an upstream that decodes `%2F` or merges `//` before it matches routes would still serve a path no middleware matched; the new `SecurityPolicy.AllowAmbiguousSlashes` forwards them exactly as the router matched them, for an upstream that keeps both. A path parameter, a `;` in any segment, is answered with `400` as well: servlet containers such as Tomcat and Jetty strip the parameters from every segment before they match routes, so `/admin;x/secret`, `/admin;/secret` and `/;/admin/secret` are `/admin/secret` there. The new `SecurityPolicy.AllowPathParameters` forwards them, for an upstream that relies on `;jsessionid`; a client can also send a literal `;` as `%3B`. A path holding a backslash, a dot segment carrying parameters (`..;`), or an escape of an unreserved character, which only a stray `%` can forge, is answered with `400` regardless. A path with dot segments is forwarded resolved, and a byte a path may not carry raw is forwarded as its escape. Every entry in `Config.Servers` must be a scheme and host only; an entry with a path, userinfo, query or fragment panics at startup with `ErrUpstreamNotOrigin`. `Balancer` answers `400 Bad Request` for an absolute-form request, such as `GET http://public.example/x`, whose `Host` header names another host or is missing: `c.Host()`, `app.Domain` and `hostauthorization` went by the host of the request line, the upstream by the `Host` header ([RFC 9112 Section 3.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112#section-3.2.2)). The two are compared without regard to case or to a default port, and only a host name or an IP address, with an optional port, can match. An application that sets the `Host` header in a middleware before `Balancer` now gets `400` for an absolute-form request whose line names another host than the one it set, and an HTTP/1.0 absolute-form request without `Host` is refused before `ModifyRequest` runs; set the upstream `Host` in `ModifyRequest` instead. `DomainForward` and `BalancerForward` keep the escapes of the routed path and of their upstream URL's path as written, so `%3B` behind `http://backend/my%20app` is no longer sent as `;`. `Balancer` also answers `400 Bad Request` for a request whose `Host` header carries userinfo and for a routed target fasthttp would read as an authority rather than a path (one that begins with `//` and holds `://`, or one beginning with `//` on a request without a `Host` header). A path override without a leading slash is forwarded rooted. Every `*fasthttp.HostClient` in a custom `Client` gets `DisablePathNormalizing` set, and behind any other `BalancingClient` a target that normalization would change is answered with `400`. Path normalization is also disabled on the default client, on a client registered with `WithClient` and on every host client a per-call client creates once the proxy has it. See [Request target](./middleware/proxy.md#request-target).

request.instructions: The documents are sections of the documentation of ONE open-source project at one commit. Report a conflict only when two sections make incompatible statements about the SAME option, flag, default value, limit, version requirement, or behavior, for the same product version and scope. These are NOT conflicts: values of different options; example values in code samples that merely override a default; statements explicitly scoped to an older version or to migration history; one section giving more detail than the other; different defaults that the text ties to different contexts (per-route vs global, dev vs build, agent mode vs server mode).
